**11. Discuss the role of ectomesenchyme in the development of melanocytes, including their origin, function, and implications for health and disease.**

Melanocytes originate from the neural crest, which gives rise to ectomesenchyme. During embryonic development, melanoblasts migrate from the neural crest to the epidermis, hair follicles, and other locations. Their primary function is melanin production, providing UV protection and determining pigmentation. Health implications include melanoma (malignant transformation), vitiligo (melanocyte destruction), and albinism (melanin synthesis defects).

**12. Discuss the role of the low-density lipoprotein receptor in the pathophysiology of familial hypercholesterolemia and cholesterol metabolism.**

The LDL receptor is crucial for cellular cholesterol uptake. It binds LDL particles, facilitating endocytosis and cholesterol delivery to cells. In familial hypercholesterolemia, mutations in the LDLR gene reduce receptor function, causing elevated plasma LDL-cholesterol, accelerated atherosclerosis, and premature cardiovascular disease. Heterozygotes have ~50% receptor function with LDL levels 2-3× normal; homozygotes have minimal function with severely elevated LDL and childhood cardiovascular events.

## Long Form Response (20 marks)

**11. Discuss the role of ectomesenchyme in the development of melanocytes, including their origin, function, and implications for health and disease.**

Melanocytes originate from the neural crest, which gives rise to ectomesenchyme. During embryonic development, melanoblasts migrate from the neural crest to the epidermis, hair follicles, and other locations. Their primary function is melanin production, providing UV protection and determining pigmentation. Health implications include melanoma (malignant transformation), vitiligo (melanocyte destruction), and albinism (melanin synthesis defects).

**12. Discuss the role of the low-density lipoprotein receptor in the pathophysiology of familial hypercholesterolemia and cholesterol metabolism.**

The LDL receptor is crucial for cellular cholesterol uptake. It binds LDL particles, facilitating endocytosis and cholesterol delivery to cells. In familial hypercholesterolemia, mutations in the LDLR gene reduce receptor function, causing elevated plasma LDL-cholesterol, accelerated atherosclerosis, and premature cardiovascular disease. Heterozygotes have ~50% receptor function with LDL levels 2-3× normal; homozygotes have minimal function with severely elevated LDL and childhood cardiovascular events.
